newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria optimistic on IMF reform funding.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria optimistic on IMF reform funding.

text.p: Bulgaria has completed its initial pledges under a $659 million reform and funding agreement with the International Monetary Fund and hopes the disbursement of the first tranche will be approved on Friday.
"I expect a favourable decision and hope that from Monday we'll be able to breathe freely," interim Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski told reporters on Thursday.
"If the IMF board approves the deal, next week we can receive $175 million," he added.
The IMF board is due to review Bulgaria's fulfillment of a list of 12 prior actions included in the agreement on Friday and decide on the disbursement of the first tranche of the funding.

Under the deal, signed last month, Bulgaria's interim cabinet pledged to prepare the introduction of a fixed exchange rate regime by the new government and parliament to be formed after April 19 general elections.
"This week is exceptionally important for the fate of Bulgarian reform," President Petar Stoyanov told reporters.
On Wednesday the European Commission said it would propose a balance of payments aid package of up to 250 million Ecus ($285 million) for Bulgaria to help fill the gap left by an IMF standby loan.

Sofia expects a further $115 million in bilateral pledges, from the Group of 24 industrialised countries. The G-24 meeting was called to help ease the effects of Bulgaria's tough reform programme on its already impoverished people.
Bulgaria's foreign debt dues this year amount to around $1 billion.
"After the elections the new reformist majority must carry out the reforms started by the caretaker government, regardless of how tough and bitter they are," said Stoyanov.

Speaking after a meeting with Stoyanov and Sofianski, Ivan Kostov, the leader of the Union of Democratic Forces, the favourite to win the elections, said his party supports the policy of the interim cabinet and will carry on with the reforms pledged under the deal.
Stoyanov said all major parties have received a copy of the IMF agreement. Broad political support was one of the IMF pre-conditions.
Under the accord Bulgaria pledged to introduce a restrictive monetary mechanism known as a currency board in June to restore confidence in its financial system.

The currency board system would require levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank and preventing the printing of money.
"After these few extremely important days we will know what size of financial backing we can rely on until the end of the year and in the first months of next year," said Sofianski.
